title: E42 - Is Legal AI in Trouble or Just Getting Started? Cosmonauts Founder, Timo Karakashev
author: Timo Karakashev

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source supports selective deployment by distinguishing broad general-model coverage from precision legal tools and by treating bundled availability as different from genuine adoption. However, its forecast that standard models may address most legal needs—especially for ordinary citizens and small businesses—and its claim that technology is the necessary route to closing the justice gap are substantially more optimistic than the cluster’s emphasis on jagged capability, verification, user capacity and remedy-level evidence.
qs: And I think that Anthropics Model, Chatchatrapity Model, those things will become better in servicing maybe 85% of legal needs out there.
But still, for the 15% of all legal needs out there, you need those point solutions.

st.an: The source is consistent with buyer-side interest and institutional adoption frictions, including budget-classification workarounds and a corporate preference to begin AI deployment in legal. However, it does not take a clear position on the cluster’s principal claims about end-to-end delivery redesign, outcome-based economics, verification, pricing pressure or apprenticeship and succession.

st.an: The source shows corporate buyer interest and a procurement workaround using a captive law firm, but it does not establish that legal departments are selectively insourcing work, becoming substitutes for outside counsel, or reducing external instructions. Its broader discussion of media visibility and public interest is largely outside the cluster’s proposition.

st.t: Legal workflows: Contextual agents remain lawyer-guided
st.an: The source establishes mainstream interest in legal AI and notes procurement barriers and divergent reactions to a hallucination sanctions incident, but it does not substantively address the cluster’s principal claims about workflow redesign, contextual integration, lawyer-guided agents or verification. Its anecdotes concern attention and demand rather than implementation or dependable legal work.

I don't think that's like a good recommendation, but I definitely think that it is the case that legal AI absolutely is part of the conversation.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source offers a relevant anecdote about procurement incentives and spending classification, but mainly argues that legal AI has entered mainstream conversation. It does not assess whether institutional absorption, workflow redesign, verification or accountability govern realised AI value.

And what you see in this coverage is that legal AI is a topic of general interest, and it is in the general conversation.

st.t: Contract infrastructure: AI challenges siloed CLM systems
st.an: The source extends the cluster’s adaptation argument by proposing a concrete basis for legal-AI product stickiness: value generated through user communities and collaborative spaces linking law firms with corporate legal customers. It does not resolve the cluster’s central CLM replacement-versus-integration dispute, and its network-effects claim remains qualitative rather than measured.
qs: That if you want to build something that many people will use, and you're not just building it for your own company, then there has to be a value to the fact that many people use it.

I think that the collaborative elements that they've introduced recently, with shared spaces, that is now allowing for the law firms to essentially offer certain usability to them for their corporate legal customers.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source accepts AI as a scalable way to augment constrained legal-service capacity and materially extends the cluster with demand-side observations about uneven adoption, procurement barriers and continued need for specialised legal tools. Its evidence is largely anecdotal and predictive, and it does not substantively address hybrid pricing, verification or autonomous delivery.
qs: So if you have been in the business where you have been beyond bandwidth or strapped for resources because your only options for intelligence was to hire more bodies, you might be a massive customer of new alternative intelligence.
But still, for the 15% of all legal needs out there, you need those point solutions.

st.t: Conditional optimism: User problems outrank AI branding
st.an: The source supports conditional, user-led optimism by identifying law-firm operations as a demand-driven opportunity beyond practice tools, while offering only qualitative reports of interest rather than proof of adoption, performance or transformation.
qs: Because we are also seeing an increased focus on utilization of technology for the business of law, not just for the practice of law.

st.t: Vendor value: Concentration forecasts face diverse competition
st.an: Abramowitz supports the cluster’s challenge to extreme concentration forecasts by arguing that Harvey and Legora currently lack adoption-driven network effects: more users do not improve their core software. He allows possible standardisation and reduced fear from wider adoption, but these caveats do not establish durable winner-takes-all advantages.
qs: Harvey as a software and Legora as a software, any of these products, I don't see any way right now in which they become more valuable based on how many people that use them.
But the core software, the core product doesn't get better if more people use it, right?

kp.k: Legal AI network effects remain uncertain
kp.d: Host Zach Abramowitz argues that Harvey and Legora do not currently become intrinsically more valuable as user numbers grow, distinguishing network effects from standardisation or reassurance through widespread adoption. He speculates that broadly sold business software may eventually require user-community value. Guest Timo Karakashev instead highlights shared workspaces connecting law firms and corporate legal clients as a source of stickiness, while conceding that they are not conceptually different from older portals.
qs: But the core software, the core product doesn't get better if more people use it, right?

I think that the collaborative elements that they've introduced recently, with shared spaces, that is now allowing for the law firms to essentially offer certain usability to them for their corporate legal customers.
I don't think that it's conceptually different.

kp.k: Premium positioning influences law firms' AI purchases
kp.d: Abramowitz interprets Harvey's positioning as a response to the profession's preference for exclusive, premium products rather than consumer ChatGPT. Karakashev similarly describes the appeal of premium interfaces but also argues for specialist precision tools. These are interpretations of customer culture and product appeal, not comparative performance findings.
qs: That's not the culture of the profession to just use what everyone else uses.
They're, the whole culture of the profession is fancy and upscale and premium.
It's like jumping into a sports car. Is it any different than any other car? It will still take you from A to B, but it's a sexy premium product.

kp.k: General-purpose AI publicity expands legal technology's audience
kp.d: Karakashev predicts that new general-purpose model announcements will not undermine specialist legal technology's growth, while increasing attention beyond the legal-tech industry. Abramowitz illustrates changing executive interest with a 2024 pharmaceutical-company CIO approaching him about beginning company AI adoption in legal, contrasting this with earlier difficulty securing legal-department technology budgets. His imagined CFO–CLO conversation about savings is a framing, not a reported customer exchange.
qs: it won't impact the potential or the growth or the impact that precision legal tech solutions have to offer to the market.
it means absolutely everything because it's putting legal tech in the spotlight yet again.
2024, I had the Chief Information Officer of a pharmaceutical company come to me and say, we'd like to begin leveraging AI and the company, right?
And he's like, and I feel like legal is a great place to get started.

kp.k: Sanctions publicity can signal capability rather than impossibility
kp.d: Abramowitz speculates that lawyers and the wider public interpreted the original ChatGPT brief-sanctions incident differently: lawyers as reassurance against automation, outsiders as evidence that AI could convincingly fool an attorney. He explicitly rejects the resulting advice against law school as a good recommendation. This is his interpretation of public reactions, not evidence of measured model reliability or public opinion.
qs: I think everyone else heard that and said, it was believable enough to really fool an attorney.
Like, I think what people kept in their heads from that story is, well, you know, don't go to law school. I don't think that's like a good recommendation

kp.k: Unmet legal needs underpin predicted market expansion
kp.d: Karakashev argues that demand exceeds supply, with ordinary people and small companies unable to obtain adequate legal support and courts congested. He predicts that innovation now aimed at the top 5% of the market will move down the value chain, describing technology as necessary to approach resolving unmet need. His suggestion that general models or new products could serve maybe 85% of legal needs, with specialist solutions needed for 15%, is an illustrative forecast rather than a measured market segmentation.
qs: people, regular people, ordinary people, small companies don't have the resources to access adequate legal support that they need.
we are part of an industry where demand completely outstrips the supply.
we are still seeing that most companies are targeting that top 5% of the market, if you wish.
those things will become better in servicing maybe 85% of legal needs out there.
But still, for the 15% of all legal needs out there, you need those point solutions.

kp.k: Affordable intelligence could create previously absent technology buyers
kp.d: Abramowitz frames AI as a scalable alternative supply of intelligence where adding people was previously the only option. He cites Trial Kit's claimed popularity among resource-constrained criminal defence attorneys facing rapidly expanding evidence volumes, arguing that affordability could unlock demand from lawyers who previously bought little technology. He asserts that evidence overload impedes professional responsibilities, but supplies no sales figures or systematic workload evidence.
qs: There's now a new supply of intelligence.
Trial Kit, which has been selling like hotcakes to criminal defense attorneys
they are not exercising their professional responsibility because they simply can't get through the amount of evidence in order to do their job.
Now the ability to have intelligence might make someone who was not a previous buyer of technology lean in very strong here.

kp.k: SaaS displacement faces deployment and service constraints
kp.d: Karakashev disputes an imminent collapse of subscription software through organisations building their own systems. Drawing on internal vibe-coding experience, he distinguishes conceptual prototypes from reliable deployment at scale and stresses training, support and continuing vendor investment. Abramowitz remains uncertain whether current exceptional software growth will persist or mask future displacement; the discussion does not resolve their differing expectations.
qs: I actually don't think that we're anywhere near that.
You know, you buy training, you buy customer support, you buy costing, you know, all wrapped up in a single product that is continuously evolving.
those are great conceptual products. But if you want to then deploy this, start utilizing it at the scale, it breaks.
My alternative question, though, is, like, is that about to come to an end and we just don't see it yet

kp.k: Australian adoption appears concentrated among leading firms
kp.d: From recent Sydney and Melbourne events, Karakashev describes maybe eight technologically advanced Australian firms—three very large international firms and five other sizable firms—whose technology journeys began decades ago. He contrasts them with smaller firms and corporate legal teams just beginning adoption. His statement that nine out of ten attendees he questioned had only Copilot and disliked it is an informal event observation without a stated sample size, not a representative survey.
qs: you have maybe eight more technologically advanced firms.
You have three firms that are really, really large, global international firms. Then you have five which are still sizable firms, and then you have everyone else.
That everyone else is all the medium and small size law firms, it's all the corporate legal teams.
Nine out of ten people will tell me, we only have Copilot and we hate it.

kp.k: Bundled AI can obstruct specialist procurement
kp.d: Karakashev attributes widespread Copilot availability partly to Microsoft 365 purchasing and suggests that executives initially resisted additional AI spending because they already paid for bundled capabilities. His account of executives citing 20–30% higher subscription costs is a hypothesised common conversation, not documented pricing research. He says dissatisfaction after a year or two prompts renewed requests for specialist tools. Both speakers criticise productivity-suite integration based on personal experience, rather than controlled comparisons.
qs: I think that this is probably the conversation that most people have had
we are paying now 20, 30% more for 365.
Why should I be paying for an additional tool?
But, you know, a year or two years in, most people are dissatisfied.
But if you're trying to use that stuff inside of, like, Google Docs or inside of an email, it's unusable.

kp.k: Talent and status pressures can precede effective utilisation
kp.d: Abramowitz argues that managing partners sometimes purchase specialist AI to avoid appearing second-rate or losing dissatisfied associates and partners. He interprets this availability-first purchasing logic as one reason firms have acquired tools without yet exploiting their capabilities fully. This is his account of procurement motivations, not measured evidence of retention effects.
qs: we can't have like our associates like walking or thinking we're second rate
People are asking for this. Get it. Get it. Whatever it's worth. I don't care if we use it or not. That should be available.
you'll understand why they weren't necessarily taken full advantage of yet, but they're there.

kp.k: IP adoption lags despite technical subject matter
kp.d: Karakashev estimates that IP technology adoption is about three years behind the broader market and describes historically conservative uptake despite early successes such as PatSnap. Abramowitz reports surprise at IP attorneys' limited understanding of transformer models and advocates teaching how AI works rather than concentrating solely on prompting. Neither provides systematic adoption or training-outcome evidence.
qs: I think that IP is maybe about three years behind.
We have no idea why the sector has been so conservative when it comes to adoption.
I'm actually teaching lawyers how the AI works
I'm always surprised when I talk with so many IP attorneys who have no basic understanding of how transformer models work.

kp.k: IP incumbent concentration shapes opportunities for new entrants
kp.d: Karakashev attributes barriers to IP technology entry to concentration around Clarivate and CPA, and claims that their merger and subsequent litigation encouraged customers to seek alternatives in search and renewals. He alleges work-channeling arrangements and payments, mentions two settlements and another ongoing case, and claims multibillion-dollar settlements without supplying case names or documentary support. These remain the guest's allegations and account of market dynamics, not established findings within the transcript.
qs: historically, the IP market has been very, very tightly held by a couple of very large players.
because there was such a huge monopoly on that market, it was very challenging for newcomers to come and meaningfully capture a piece of that market.
a lot of large law firms have been essentially channeling work to this mega company in exchange of under the table payments.
There's like a multi-billion-dollar settlements that were done on the back of that.
There was a desire to seek alternative to what was considered the constant in that space.

kp.k: Specialist IP workflows offer further expansion opportunities
kp.d: Karakashev identifies patent drafting, renewals, translations, litigation and requests for proposals as opportunities, particularly internationally, while describing uptake as comparatively slow. He recounts Legora's early IP focus and patent-related demonstrations in 2023, and argues that capital is necessary for specialist providers to expand and take products to market. This supports his expectation of more entrants, rather than establishing whether independent IP vendors will survive or be acquired.
qs: There is opportunity in patent drafting. There is opportunity in renewals. There is opportunity in translations. There is opportunity in litigation.
There is an opportunity in RFPs, for example, for request for proposals.
some of the early demos that Max was actually showing back in 2023 were all around patent drafting and patent processing
there is still a lot of opportunity that hasn't been harvested, especially in the broader market internationally.
you do need capital to meaningfully expand.

kp.k: Practitioner involvement should deepen technology implementation discussions
kp.d: Karakashev argues that legal technology discussions too often involve innovation and knowledge teams rather than the lawyers using the products. He recommends more practice-specific engagement with end users, describing the United States and UK as sufficiently mature markets for deeper conversations about technology's implications for particular areas of practice.
qs: You have the innovation team, you have the knowledge teams, but you rarely have the end utilizers of technology.
Let's not forget that the technology is being built for the practitioners.

We now have enough history to be able to involve the actual legal practitioners to get together with some of those point solutions and have more in-depth conversation around what technology means for their area of operation.

kp.k: AI interest extends from legal practice to operations
kp.d: Karakashev reports increased interest in technology for running legal organisations, distinguishing law-firm operations from corporate legal operations. He says vendors including Harvey and Legora show interest in extending practice-oriented tools toward broader organisational uses. Abramowitz separately reports law-firm requests to improve firm operations and identifies this as a substantial opportunity; neither describes measured operational outcomes.
qs: we are also seeing an increased focus on utilization of technology for the business of law, not just for the practice of law.
we are seeing some interest even from players such as Harvey and Legora
we've spent all this emphasis on practice of law. What about operating our firm better?

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Timo Karakashev predicts continued growth for specialist legal AI alongside improving general models, with broader access to legal help as the larger opportunity.
pts.d: Karakashev describes Harvey and Legora as effective products whose recent shared spaces let law firms extend functionality to corporate legal customers. He accepts that these spaces are not conceptually different from older portals, but argues that premium presentation makes users more interested in trying them. He argues that new general-model announcements do not undermine specialist legal technology's growth potential and instead increase wider attention to the sector. He predicts that innovation currently concentrated at the top of the legal market will spread downwards, addressing demand that exceeds available legal-service supply. His suggestion that general models or new products could serve roughly 85% of legal needs, leaving 15% for specialist solutions, is explicitly tentative rather than a measured market split. He rejects an imminent demise of subscription software through vibe coding, arguing that scalable deployment, support, training and ongoing improvement remain valuable. He also identifies growing opportunities for specialist IP tools and for technology supporting law-firm operations rather than only legal practice.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Karakashev relies primarily on product use, conference conversations and commercial experience, not formal performance studies or representative market data.
pts.d: For Harvey and Legora, he cites recent demonstrations and internal use; both also sponsored his Australian events. His account of early adoption and dissatisfaction with Copilot comes from conversations with attendees in Sydney and Melbourne, supplemented by his own experience with an earlier version of Copilot. The 'nine out of ten' statement describes those conversations, not a documented market survey. His skepticism about replacing SaaS with internally generated software rests partly on his company's experience of vibe-coded prototypes breaking at scale. He contrasts falling valuations at some established companies with claimed rapid recurring-revenue growth at unnamed private providers, acknowledging that their detailed performance is not publicly observable. His IP account draws on industry experience and examples of vendors, investment and incumbent-market developments; his allegations concerning incumbent litigation and settlements are not accompanied by case references. No benchmark, measured legal-outcome study or quantified access-to-justice evidence supports the proposed 85%/15% division or the predicted downward diffusion of benefits.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The 2026 conversation portrays legal AI as an early-stage market, with uneven adoption and no fixed deadline for broad public benefits.
pts.d: Karakashev describes current vendor targeting as concentrated on approximately the top 5% of the market and says benefits will 'eventually' reach lower market segments, without supplying a date. He presents the 85%/15% division as a possibility. In Australia, he distinguishes roughly eight technologically advanced firms, whose investment began decades earlier, from smaller firms and corporate departments whose journeys are only beginning. He says dissatisfaction with bundled AI becomes apparent a year or two into use, but qualifies his own assessment of Copilot by acknowledging that he does not know whether it has been fixed. He estimates that IP adoption is about three years behind, while describing increased interest and capital as conditions enabling specialist providers to expand. He argues that widespread replacement of SaaS by self-built systems is not near-term because users lack deployment capacity, time or expertise and because prototypes do not necessarily scale. He identifies the US and UK as sufficiently mature for more practitioner-specific conversations about legal technology.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted effects extend from large firms and corporate legal buyers to underserved individuals, small companies, IP practitioners and operational teams.
pts.d: Large law firms and enterprises are the initial beneficiaries of efficiency and modernization, while shared legal-AI workspaces connect firms with their corporate legal clients. Karakashev presents ordinary people and small companies unable to afford adequate legal support as the principal prospective beneficiaries of wider diffusion, distinguishing this unmet need from enterprise efficiency gains. Australian medium and small firms and corporate legal teams represent a largely early-stage adoption market in his account. He describes CFOs and other executives initially directing legal teams toward bundled Microsoft tools rather than funding specialist purchases, followed by dissatisfied users seeking dedicated alternatives. IP practitioners and specialist providers face opportunities in drafting patents, renewals, translations, litigation and requests for proposals. Finally, he says attention is expanding to law-firm operations and corporate legal operations, with vendors interested in reaching functions beyond legal practitioners, including HR.
